That tax is paid from cash that would otherwise earn 2.5% after tax. Units grow 5% a year and are all sold in year 10. In a TFSA, RRSP or other registered plan none of this tax arises. Why the TFSA limit is stuck at $7,000, and when it moves: inflation indexing in $500 steps

Section 117.1 sets the yearly factor. It divides the average CPI for the 12 months ending on 30 September before the year by the average for the 12 months before that, subtracts one, and rounds to the nearest 0.1%. The same factors index the federal tax brackets and many credits, which is why the TFSA step and the bracket increase are announced together each autumn.

Section 207.01 of the Income Tax Act defines the “TFSA dollar limit”. For 2009 to 2012 it was $5,000; for 2013 and 2014, $5,500; for 2015, $10,000. For every year after 2015 it is “$5,000 adjusted for each year after 2009” under section 117.1, rounded to the nearest multiple of $500, with an exact tie rounded up. CRA’s indexation page describes the same rule: the limit is fixed at $5,000, indexed for each year after 2009 and rounded to the nearest $500.

CRA’s guidance on mutual funds explains why. Distributions are taxed while you own the units, and if you reinvest them you must still report them, because you are considered to have received them before reinvesting. Reinvesting buys more units, which raises your average cost per unit. The early buyer’s cost base is $21,600 against the later buyer’s $20,000. That higher cost base is the record of the tax already paid.

Distinguish new pay from an existing lump sum. Saving from each paycheque grows with income and the limit rises occasionally; moving an existing non-registered holding into a TFSA is a different decision, because transferring units in kind is a disposition at market value. The in-kind contribution guide covers it.

Do not let tax drive the choice of fund. Diversification, fees, risk and the time until you need the money matter more than one distribution. Returns are uncertain; a fund bought after its distribution can still fall.

In a taxable account, compare a few days with the cost. If the record date is days away and the estimated distribution is large, waiting for it to pass is a reasonable, low-cost habit. Waiting weeks or months to save a cost of this size is market timing, and missing a rise could easily cost more; the waiting-for-a-dip guide shows how cash rules drift.

Index your own contributions, not just the room. If your plan is to save a fixed share of income, the inflation-adjusted contribution guide shows why a flat dollar amount loses ground over decades. The RRSP and TFSA comparison covers which account to fill first.

Inside a registered account, ignore it. In a TFSA, RRSP, RRIF, RESP or FHSA the distribution is not taxed when paid. The account’s rules, not the fund, decide that: a fund is not tax-exempt in itself.

Keep the account and the investment separate. Income and gains earned inside a TFSA are generally not taxed and withdrawals are not taxable, but those are account rules. A balanced fund held in a TFSA is still exposed to market falls, fund fees and uncertain returns. The asset location guide compares what to hold where.
Keep the cash for the tax. A reinvested distribution produces no cash. The tax cash provision guide shows how to set money aside for it.

Keep the cost base records. Reinvested distributions raise your adjusted cost base. Many platforms track it, but CRA expects you to calculate it for each fund and series. Missing the reinvested amounts means paying tax twice on the same money when you sell.

Know your own room. The yearly limit is only one part. Unused room carries forward; amounts withdrawn are added back on 1 January of the following year; and over-contributions are taxed at 1% a month. The TFSA recontribution calendar follows those rules. Losses inside the account do not restore room; the loss and room guide shows why.
A December purchase and a February tax slip

A distribution paid days after you buy hands part of your own money back as taxable income. Follow the same purchase made just before and just after the distribution: identical units and value, a higher cost base, tax paid now and partly won back later. See how the cost depends on distribution size, its tax character and how long you hold.

A fund distribution can be capital gains, Canadian dividends, foreign income, interest, other income or return of capital, or a mix, and the T3 or T5 slip says which. Each is taxed differently. Capital gains are half included in income. Interest and foreign income are fully taxed. Eligible Canadian dividends get the gross-up and dividend tax credit. Return of capital is not taxed now; it lowers the cost base instead.

A fund that distributes little and grows mostly through unrealized gains defers tax for its holders in general, which is one reason fund turnover and distribution history matter for non-registered accounts beyond the December question.

A fund’s unit price is its net asset value per unit. When the fund pays a distribution, that cash leaves the fund, so the unit price falls by the distribution, all else being equal. With the defaults, $20,000 buys units just before a distribution of 8% of the price. The distribution is $1,600 and the units are then worth $18,400. Reinvested at the lower price, the $1,600 buys more units, and the holding is back to $20,000.
A higher limit adds room on 1 January. It does not change room you already have, does not raise the limit on past years, and does not make any investment inside the account safer or more rewarding.

Added up, the $109,000 of limits from 2009 to 2026 is worth about $138,617 in September 2026 prices. If you turned 18 after 2009, enter your age; someone aged 29 at the end of 2026, first eligible in 2015, has $78,000 of limits worth about $94,148. These totals describe room, not wealth. Room only becomes wealth when money is contributed and invested, and they apply only to someone who has been 18 or older and resident in Canada in every year counted.

At 2% a year, the limit reaches $8,000 in four years, $9,000 in ten and $10,000 in sixteen. At 1% a year it takes seven years to reach $8,000 and thirty to reach $10,000. Each $500 step needs the unrounded amount to grow by about $500, which is around 7% of the current limit, so at 2% inflation a step arrives roughly every three to four years.

Because the early buyer’s cost base is $1,600 higher, their capital gain on sale is $1,600 smaller. At half inclusion and 29.65%, that saves $237.20 of tax in the year of sale, whatever the sale price. If the units are sold for less than cost, the same $1,600 enlarges a capital loss instead.

Because the law compounds the unrounded amount, not the rounded limit, these gaps do not build up. A year when rounding gives less room is not carried forward as a deficit, and a generous year is not taken back. Over many years the published limits track the indexed amount closely; the bars bounce within $250 either side of zero.

Buy a non-registered fund just before its distribution, or just after?

Buying a fund in a taxable account just before a distribution does not lose you any investment value, but it pulls tax forward. The cost base rises by the distribution, so part of that tax comes back when you sell. The lasting cost is the growth on the tax cash and, if the distribution is income rather than capital gains, the difference in tax rates. It is usually modest, it is zero in a TFSA or RRSP, and it is rarely worth staying out of the market for long to avoid.

Large year-end distributions usually come from funds that sold appreciated holdings during the year, for example after a strong market, a manager change or heavy redemptions by other investors. Fund companies often publish estimated year-end distributions in November or early December, with a record date that decides who receives them. Checking the estimate before a large December purchase is cheap; the actual amount and its character are confirmed only on the tax slip.

The TFSA dollar limit is $5,000 indexed to inflation since 2009, rounded to the nearest $500. This guide rebuilds the limit from the law, year by year, using the same consumer price index the law uses. It then answers four practical questions: why the limit sits still and then jumps, how much the room has really been worth, what the 2027 figure is likely to be, and how quickly future steps come under different inflation rates. The tool below lets you change your age, which sets your first eligible year, the inflation you assume after 2027 and how far ahead to look.

Treat this as a calculation, not an announcement. When this page was checked on 26 October 2026, CRA’s limits page listed TFSA limits only to 2026 and CRA’s indexation page showed factors only to 2026. Section 117.1 also allows the CPI to be “adjusted in such manner as may be prescribed”. The margin here is wide: the unrounded amount would need to fall below $7,250 to keep the limit at $7,000, which would take a factor of 0.9% or less. Even so, contribute based on CRA’s published figure and your own room in My Account, not on this projection.

Two features matter. First, the unrounded amount keeps compounding every year, whether or not the published limit moves. Second, the 2013–2014 and 2015 limits were written directly into the law, so they sit above or off the indexed path. Since 2016 every limit has been the rounded indexed amount.

Why the distribution is your own money coming back

Year 0 is a sale immediately after the distribution: the higher cost base creates a capital loss that offsets $237 of tax. The later the sale, the longer the tax cash has been missing and the less a dollar of future tax saving is worth today. Because part of the distribution is taxed as income in full but recovered only as a half-included capital loss or smaller gain, the cost never falls to zero.
